sheets.title: The rules, and the chain rule that matters most
sheets.body:
The power rule \( \dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1} \) does the routine work, and differentiation is linear — constants pass through, sums differentiate term by term. Together those handle every polynomial.

Products need more care. The product rule is \( (uv)' = u'v + uv' \), read ‘u v all prime equals u prime v plus u v prime’. Multiplying the two derivatives is simply wrong, and the reason is physical: when both quantities vary, the product changes because the first moved while the second held, and because the second moved while the first held. Two contributions, two terms. The quotient rule \( \left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2} \) has the same shape with a minus sign, so the order of its two products is not interchangeable.

The chain rule handles a function of a function, which in engineering is the normal case. In Leibniz form it is \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du}\dfrac{du}{dx} \), read ‘d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x’, where \( u \) is the inner function. The differentials appear to cancel, which is not a proof but is a reliable memory aid that extends to longer chains.

The working method. Name the inner function in writing. Differentiate the outer while treating the inner as one symbol. Multiply by the inner derivative. Substitute back.

Almost every chain-rule error is at the first step. Differentiating \( e^{-t/12} \) as though the exponent were \( -t \), and so losing the factor of one twelfth, gives an answer twelve times too large with no visible symptom. One derivative to carry forward: the exponential is its own derivative, \( \dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x} = e^{x} \), and with the chain rule that single fact generates every growth and decay rate in the next lesson.

examples.title: A cooling curve, and a product where the terms fight
examples.body:
Problem 1. A component cools as \( T(t) = 20 + 60e^{-t/12} \), \( T \) in °C and \( t \) in minutes. Find \( dT/dt \) at \( t = 0 \) and \( t = 12 \).

Approach. The constant differentiates to zero; the rest is an exponential of a function, so name the inner function first: \( u = -t/12 \), giving \( -1/12 \). Forgetting that factor overstates every cooling rate twelvefold, so write it down rather than carry it.

Solution. The derivative of \( 60e^{u} \) with respect to \( u \) is \( 60e^{u} \); multiplying along the chain gives \( dT/dt = -5e^{-t/12} \). At \( t = 0 \) that is \( -5 \); at \( t = 12 \), \( -5e^{-1} = -1.84 \).

Answer. Cooling at 5°C/min initially, 1.84°C/min after twelve minutes. Negative throughout, as any cooling curve must be.

Problem 2. During run-up a drive's torque rises as \( M = 50 + 2t \) N·m while speed falls as \( \omega = 100 - 0.5t \) rad/s. Power is \( P = M\omega \). Find \( dP/dt \) at \( t = 10\ \mathrm{s} \).

Approach. Both factors vary, so this is a product rule. The two contributions have opposite signs — torque helping, speed hurting — so the answer is a competition whose sign cannot be guessed. The shortcut of multiplying derivatives gives \( -1 \): not merely inaccurate but the wrong sign.

Solution. \( M' = 2 \), \( \omega' = -0.5 \); at \( t = 10 \), \( M = 70 \) and \( \omega = 95 \). So \( dP/dt = 2(95) + 70(-0.5) = 190 - 35 \).

Answer. \( 155\ \mathrm{W/s} \) — rising, because torque outweighs speed at this instant. It need not stay so as the run-up continues.

5.lecture:
§1 · The function that is its own derivative

One function grows at a rate equal to its own size: \( \frac{d}{dt}e^{t} = e^{t} \). Scale time by a constant and \( \frac{d}{dt}e^{kt} = k e^{kt} \): growth or decay proportional to the current amount. That single property makes \( e^{kt} \) the native language of charging capacitors, cooling castings, decaying vibration transients, draining accumulators, and compounding costs.

§2 · Decay with an offset — the plant's favorite curve

A hot object doesn't decay to zero; it decays to ambient. The working form is

\[ T(t) = T_\infty + (T_0 - T_\infty)\,e^{-t/\tau} \tag{1} \]

where \( \tau \) is the time constant: after one \( \tau \), 63% of the gap to ambient is closed; after 3\( \tau \), 95%; after 5\( \tau \), it's over. Ask "how many time constants?" and any first-order transient becomes readable at a glance.

§3 · Logarithms — solving for time

The logarithm inverts the exponential; it is how you extract when:

\[ t = \tau \,\ln\!\frac{T_0 - T_\infty}{T(t) - T_\infty} \tag{2} \]

Logs also compress scale (decibels, pH, Richter) and straighten exponentials: plot \( \ln(T - T_\infty) \) against \( t \) and first-order data falls on a line whose slope is \( -1/\tau \). Fitting a straight line to a log plot is how you measure a time constant from plant data.

§4 · The transient protocol

Every first-order transient yields to the same four questions, asked in order. What is the destination? Identify \( T_\infty \) — ambient, setpoint, asymptote — because everything is measured as a gap from it. What is the gap? Compute the current excess over the destination; the transient's whole story is this gap shrinking. What is the tempo? Get \( \tau \) — from a datasheet, from a fit, or from data via the semilog method of §3: plot \( \ln(\text{gap}) \) against time, and the slope is \( -1/\tau \). When? Turn any target into time with \( t = \tau\,\ln(\text{gap}_0/\text{gap}_{target}) \), or count in the coarse currency — one \( \tau \) closes 63% of the gap, three close 95%, five end the story.

The same machinery runs upward for growth. Compounding at rate \( r \) per period doubles in \( \ln 2/\ln(1+r) \) periods — the honest version of the rule of 70 — and any quantity that grows in proportion to itself, from an escalating tariff to a fouling deposit, is the exponential wearing different clothes. When data arrives, straighten it first: if the semilog plot is not a line, the process is not first-order, and no amount of \( \tau \)-talk will make it one. The plot is the test; the constants come after.

Know the honest failure modes too. A curve on the semilog plot usually means two time constants stacked — a fast surface effect riding on a slow bulk one — and a flat early section means deadtime: transport delay before the response begins. Both are information, not nuisance. Report what the data shows, fit the region the model genuinely describes, and say so; a stated approximation is engineering, an unstated one is luck.

Closing. \( e^{kt} \) encodes self-proportional change; \( \tau \) makes transients countable; logarithms solve for time and straighten curves so data confesses its constants.
5.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Chain rule (Lesson 4) — \( \tfrac{d}{dt}e^{-t/\tau} = -\tfrac{1}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau} \).
  • Log laws — \( \ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b \), \( \ln e^x = x \).
  • Limits (Lesson 2) — \( e^{-t/\tau}\to 0 \): the transient's destiny is ambient.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use
Exponential change\( \tfrac{d}{dt}e^{kt} = k\,e^{kt} \)Any quantity whose rate is proportional to its size — growth or decay.
First-order transient\( T = T_\infty + (T_0 - T_\infty)e^{-t/\tau} \)Cooling, charging, draining — decay to an offset destination.
Time constant\( \tau \): 63% per \( \tau \), 95% by \( 3\tau \)Reading any transient's tempo at a glance.
Solving for time\( t = \tau\ln\tfrac{T_0 - T_\infty}{T - T_\infty} \)When the question is when, not what.
Half-life\( t_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2 \approx 0.693\tau \)Halving language for decays; never equal to \( \tau \) itself.
Semilog straightening\( \ln(T - T_\infty) \) vs \( t \), slope \( -1/\tau \)Measuring \( \tau \) from data — and testing whether first-order applies at all.

5.kuwait: Vignette — how long until we can touch it? You arrive at a melt-shop planning meeting: a repair crew needs billets on the cooling bed handled "as soon as possible." The shift engineer guesses; you fit instead. Two historian points — 620 °C at 30 min, 259 °C at 60 min — on a semilog plot of \( T-30 \) give a straight line whose slope yields \( \tau \approx 45 \) min, and equation (2) turns that into a committed answer: just under two hours to 100 °C. Scheduling gets a number with a derivation behind it instead of a shrug, and nobody gloves up against a 260-degree surface.

quiz.q:
Billet cooling window

Problem. A steel billet leaves a cooling bed model at \( T_0 = 900\ \mathrm{°C} \) into \( T_\infty = 30\ \mathrm{°C} \) surroundings with \( \tau = 45 \) min (representative first-order fit). Find: temperature after 60 min, and the time to reach 100 °C for safe handling.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( T(60) = 30 + 870\,e^{-60/45} = 30 + 870\,e^{-1.333} \). (2) \( e^{-1.333} = 0.264 \Rightarrow T(60) = 30 + 229 = 259\ \mathrm{°C} \). (3) For 100 °C, equation (2): \( t = 45 \ln\frac{870}{70} = 45 \ln 12.43 = 45 \times 2.52 = 113\ \mathrm{min} \).

Answer: ≈259 °C after an hour; ≈113 min (≈2.5\( \tau \)) to 100 °C. Sanity check: 100 °C sits 92% of the way to ambient, and 2.5 time constants closes ~92% of the gap. Internally consistent.

quiz.q:
Doubling time from a growth rate

Problem. Plant electricity tariff escalates 3% per year. Find: the doubling time of the bill at constant consumption.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Growth: \( C = C_0(1.03)^n \). Doubling when \( (1.03)^n = 2 \). (2) \( n = \ln 2 / \ln 1.03 = 0.6931 / 0.02956 = 23.4 \) years.

Answer: ≈23 years. Sanity check: the rule of 70 gives \( 70/3 \approx 23.3 \) — the shortcut and the logarithm agree.

quiz.q:
A fouling filter on the calendar

Problem. A filter's differential pressure grows 5% per week from a clean-condition \( \Delta P_0 = 0.30 \) bar. The changeout alarm is set at 0.60 bar. Find: how many weeks until the alarm, assuming the compounding trend holds.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Model: \( \Delta P = 0.30\,(1.05)^n \). Alarm when \( (1.05)^n = 2 \). (2) Take logarithms: \( n = \ln 2/\ln 1.05 = 0.6931/0.04879 = 14.2 \) weeks.

Answer: ≈14 weeks — a doubling time, read straight off the growth rate. Sanity check: the rule of 70 gives \( 70/5 = 14 \) — shortcut and logarithm agree, so the maintenance plan can commit to a changeout window around week 13 with margin.

quiz.q: A thermocouple with first-order time constant \( \tau = 8\ \mathrm{s} \) reads 20 °C when it is plunged into an oil bath held at 80 °C. What does it read 12 s later?
quiz.solution: The first-order response is \( T(t) = T_\infty + (T_0 - T_\infty)e^{-t/\tau} = 80 - 60\,e^{-1.5} \approx 66.6 \) °C. The 57.8 °C distractor applies the one-time-constant 63% rule to an interval of \( 1.5\tau \); that figure holds only at exactly one \( \tau \). 110 °C extrapolates the initial rate linearly, ignoring that the driving gap shrinks as the reading approaches the bath, and 33.4 °C swaps the roles of \( T_0 \) and \( T_\infty \).

quiz.q: A casting's cooling transient is logged and \( \ln(T - T_\infty) \) is plotted against time; the points fall on a straight line of slope \( -0.040\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} \). What is the half-life of the transient, i.e. the time for the remaining temperature gap to halve?
quiz.solution: The semilog slope equals \( -1/\tau \), so \( \tau = 1/0.040 = 25 \) min, and the half-life is \( t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2 \approx 17.3 \) min. Choosing 25 min confuses the time constant (63% of the gap closed) with the half-life (50% closed). 36.1 min inverts the relation as \( \tau/\ln 2 \), and 12.5 min guesses \( \tau/2 \) in place of \( \tau \ln 2 \).

quiz.q: A first-order transient has run for exactly three time constants. Roughly what fraction of the initial gap to the destination remains?
quiz.solution: The remaining fraction decays as \( e^{-t/\tau} \); at \( t = 3\tau \) that is \( e^{-3} \approx 0.050 \) — about 5% left, 95% closed. Answering 63% or 37% swaps the closed and remaining fractions at one time constant into the wrong slot; 95% states what is done, not what remains. The 63/95/99 ladder at \( 1\tau/3\tau/5\tau \) is worth owning cold — it is the transient-reading currency of every discipline downstream.

quiz.q: You must confirm that a cooling trend is first-order and extract its time constant graphically. Which plot renders the data straight, and what does its slope encode?
choices: \( \ln T \) versus \( t \); the slope is \( -1/\tau \)
\( \ln(T - T_\infty) \) versus \( t \); the slope is \( -1/\tau \)
\( \ln(T - T_\infty) \) versus \( t \); the slope is \( -\tau \)
\( T \) versus \( \ln t \); the slope is \( -1/\tau \)
quiz.solution: Since \( T - T_\infty = (T_0 - T_\infty)e^{-t/\tau} \), taking logarithms gives \( \ln(T - T_\infty) = \ln(T_0 - T_\infty) - t/\tau \): a straight line in \( t \) with slope \( -1/\tau \). Plotting \( \ln T \) without subtracting ambient is the classic error — the offset \( T_\infty \) leaves the curve bent, because the pure exponential is the gap, not the temperature itself. A slope of \( -\tau \) inverts the fingerprint, and \( T \) versus \( \ln t \) straightens logarithmic trends, not exponential ones.

quiz.q: For a first-order transient, how long does closing 99% of the gap take, expressed in time constants?
quiz.solution: Requiring \( e^{-t/\tau} = 0.01 \) gives \( t = \tau\ln 100 \approx 4.6\,\tau \) — the origin of the field rule that five time constants end the story. \( \tau\ln 10 \) closes only 90%; \( \tau\ln 2 \) is the half-life; and \( 99\tau \) misreads the exponential as linear, the very misreading the time-constant idea exists to prevent.

5.recap:
• \( e^x \) is its own derivative; exponential behaviour is what happens whenever the rate of change is proportional to the amount currently present.
  • The plant's standard curve is decay toward an offset, not toward zero: something approaches a final value \( y_\infty \) rather than vanishing.
  • The time constant \( \tau \) is the whole story: about 63% of the journey is complete after one \( \tau \), 95% after three, 99% after five.
  • Logarithms are how you solve for time — "when will it reach X" is a logarithm, every time.
  • Transient protocol: identify the initial value, the final value, and \( \tau \). With those three, the curve is fully determined.

intro.what: Exponential behaviour appears wherever a quantity's rate of change is proportional to the quantity itself — cooling, discharge, vibration decay, corrosion allowance, radioactive sources. The logarithm is its inverse, and it is the tool that turns a multiplicative process into a straight line you can read. This lesson gives both, and the two time constants engineers actually quote.
keypoints: Exponential change means the rate is proportional to the amount present, which is why it never quite reaches zero.
\( e^{x} \) is its own derivative; every growth and decay rate follows from that one fact and the chain rule.
Decay is written \( A_0e^{-t/\tau} \), where the time constant is the time to fall to about 37% of the start.
The half-life is the time to halve, and it is a fixed multiple of the time constant: \( t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2 \).
Logarithms turn products into sums, which is why they linearise multiplicative data and why decibels exist.
A straight line on a log axis is an exponential on a linear one — the quickest way to identify the behaviour from plant data.
Solving for time means taking a logarithm of both sides, so the natural log is the working tool rather than a curiosity.

sheets.title: Exponentials, and the logarithm that undoes them
sheets.body:
A great many industrial quantities share one behaviour: the rate of change is proportional to how much is left. A hot component loses heat fastest when hottest, a vessel discharges fastest when fullest. Whenever that proportionality holds the curve is an exponential, because \( e^{x} \) is the one function equal to its own derivative and the chain rule supplies the constant.

Decay is \( A = A_0e^{-t/\tau} \), read ‘A equals A nought e to the minus t over tau’, with \( A_0 \) the initial value and the time constant \( \tau \) the time to fall to \( 1/e \), about 37%, of the start. Since the rate shrinks with the amount, the curve never reaches zero — which is why a purge is specified as five time constants rather than ‘until empty’.

Engineers more often quote the half-life, and the two are rigidly linked by \( t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2 \), about 0.693 of the time constant. Neither depends on where you start measuring: the time to halve is the same from any point on the curve, which is what makes the number worth quoting.

The natural logarithm \( \ln x \) inverts the exponential, and its working purpose is narrow: when the unknown sits in an exponent, taking logarithms brings it down where algebra can reach it. Every ‘how long until’ question is answered this way.

Its second use is diagnostic. Logarithms turn products into sums, so a process multiplying by a fixed factor per unit time plots as a straight line on a logarithmic axis — the quickest test available on plant data, with the slope giving the time constant directly. The same property explains the decibel \( 10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1) \): every 10 dB is one factor of ten in power, and because it is a ratio the figure is meaningless until the reference is stated.

examples.title: Time constant from two readings, and a ratio in decibels
examples.body:
Problem 1. A machine's vibration amplitude is 12 mm when the drive trips and 3 mm eight seconds later. Find the time constant and half-life, and predict the amplitude at 20 s.

Approach. Two readings and one assumed shape fix the curve: substitute into \( A = A_0e^{-t/\tau} \) and take logarithms to release \( \tau \). Form the check first — 12 to 3 is two halvings in eight seconds, so the half-life must be 4 s. The commonest error is a dropped minus sign, which returns a negative time constant and a growing curve.

Solution. \( 3 = 12e^{-8/\tau} \) gives \( e^{-8/\tau} = 0.25 \), so \( -8/\tau = \ln 0.25 = -1.386 \) and \( \tau = 5.77\ \mathrm{s} \). Then \( t_{1/2} = 5.77 \times 0.693 = 4.00\ \mathrm{s} \), matching the check, and 20 s is five half-lives, so \( 12/2^5 \).

Answer. \( \tau = 5.77\ \mathrm{s} \), \( t_{1/2} = 4.00\ \mathrm{s} \), 0.375 mm at 20 s.

Problem 2. A modification raises radiated sound power by a factor of 100. Express it in decibels. Separately, what power ratio is a 3 dB rise?

Approach. The first part substitutes into the definition; the second runs it backwards, undoing a logarithm rather than taking one. The classic error is treating decibels as additive in the quantity: 20 dB is not twice 10 dB in power, it is ten times it.

Solution. \( 10\log_{10}(100) = 20 \). Backwards, \( \log_{10}(P_2/P_1) = 0.3 \), so the ratio is \( 10^{0.3} \).

Answer. 20 dB; and 3 dB is a doubling of power — worth memorising, since it recurs as a bandwidth and margin criterion.

6.lecture:
§1 · Where curves turn

A smooth function can only reverse direction where its derivative is zero. Those points — where \( f'(x) = 0 \) — are the critical points, and among them live the maxima and minima that engineering actually cares about: least material, least energy, most throughput. The second derivative classifies them: \( f'' > 0 \) cups upward (minimum), \( f'' < 0 \) caps downward (maximum).

§2 · The optimization recipe

Every optimization in this course follows one recipe:

\[ \text{model} \to \text{constraint} \to \text{single-variable objective} \to f'(x)=0 \to \text{check ends} \tag{1} \]

Write the quantity to optimize; use the constraint to eliminate variables; differentiate; solve; then — the step everyone forgets — check the boundary. In a plant, optima frequently live at the constraint (valve fully open, maximum allowed speed) rather than at an interior zero of the derivative. The mathematics is honest about this only if you ask.

§3 · A worked shape decision

Minimum-surface tanks, minimum-loss pipe runs, maximum-volume boxes from fixed sheet — these classic problems all reduce to recipe (1). In §Worked Examples we size an open-top square tank for 4 m³ with least plate area — the kind of trade a fabrication shop quotes weekly — and find the optimum has height equal to half the base side, a proportion worth memorizing.

§4 · From words to optimum — the translation discipline

The calculus in recipe (1) is the easy half; the profession lives in the translation that precedes it. Practice the sequence deliberately. Name the objective — the single quantity to minimize or maximize — and write its formula with every variable it depends on. Name the constraint — the fixed volume, the required duty, the forbidden region — as an equation, and use it to eliminate variables until the objective depends on one. Differentiate, set to zero, solve — then classify with the second derivative, and walk the boundary: evaluate the objective at every end of the allowed interval, because constrained optima are the plant's normal case, not its exception. Finally, sanity-check the geometry of the answer: optima usually land on proportions — height equals half the base, cost terms equal at the minimum — and a result that looks arbitrary is a result worth re-deriving.

Two honest cautions. A mathematical optimum is only as good as the model's costs: a plate that is cheapest by area may not be cheapest by welding length, and writing the model down makes that assumption visible and challengeable. And when the objective is nearly flat near its optimum — as it often is — precision fetishism wastes effort: report the flat region, not a false fourth digit.

Real decision variables are also rarely continuous. Batches come in integers, plate comes in stock sizes, speeds come in motor steps. The calculus still earns its keep: find the continuous optimum, then evaluate the objective at the feasible values on either side of it and take the better — the curve's flatness near the optimum usually makes the rounding cost negligible, and computing it proves that instead of assuming it.

Closing. Derivative zero finds candidates; the second derivative sorts them; the boundary check keeps you honest. Optimization is calculus with a purchase order attached.

6.kuwait: Vignette — the cheapest tank in the yard. You arrive at a fabricator's estimating office with three quotes for the same 4 m³ rinse tank, each a different shape. The estimator prices plate by the square metre; nobody has asked what shape minimizes metres. Twenty minutes of Lesson-6 calculus — worked example 1 verbatim — shows the 2 × 2 × 1 proportion saves plate against both taller quotes, and the shop standardizes the proportion for the whole small-tank family. Optimization didn't need software; it needed someone to write \( A' = 0 \).

quiz.q:
Least steel for a square tank

Problem. A fabrication shop must build an open-top, square-base tank holding \( V = 4\ \mathrm{m^3} \). Find: base side \( x \) and height \( h \) minimizing plate area.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Objective: \( A = x^2 + 4xh \) (base + four walls). (2) Constraint: \( x^2 h = 4 \Rightarrow h = 4/x^2 \). (3) Substitute: \( A(x) = x^2 + 16/x \). (4) Differentiate: \( A' = 2x - 16/x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x^3 = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2\ \mathrm{m} \), so \( h = 1\ \mathrm{m} \). (5) Classify: \( A'' = 2 + 32/x^3 > 0 \) → minimum. \( A = 4 + 8 = 12\ \mathrm{m^2} \).

Answer: 2 m × 2 m base, 1 m high; 12 m² of plate. Sanity check: nudge to \( x = 1.8 \): \( A = 3.24 + 8.89 = 12.13\ \mathrm{m^2} \) — worse, as a minimum demands.

quiz.q:
The boundary wins

Problem. Pump energy cost falls with impeller trim \( x \) (%) as \( E(x) = 100 - 1.2x \) while vibration risk cost rises as \( R(x) = 0.05x^2 \); trims beyond 15% are forbidden by the OEM. Find: the trim minimizing total cost \( C = E + R \) on \( [0, 15] \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( C(x) = 100 - 1.2x + 0.05x^2 \). (2) \( C' = -1.2 + 0.1x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 12 \) — interior candidate, \( C(12) = 100 - 14.4 + 7.2 = 92.8 \). (3) Check ends: \( C(0) = 100 \), \( C(15) = 100 - 18 + 11.25 = 93.25 \).

Answer: trim 12% (interior optimum beats both boundaries). Sanity check: \( C'' = 0.1 > 0 \) confirms a minimum; had the OEM cap been 10%, the answer would have been the boundary, 10% — recipe (1)'s final step earning its keep.

quiz.q:
The batch size that balances two costs

Problem. Producing a part in batches of size \( x \) costs, per part, \( C(x) = 400/x + 0.25x \) — the first term spreads a fixed setup cost, the second carries inventory. Find: the batch size minimizing cost per part, the minimum cost, and the structural property of the optimum.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( C'(x) = -400/x^2 + 0.25 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 1600 \Rightarrow x = 40 \). (2) \( C(40) = 10 + 10 = 20 \) per part; \( C''(x) = 800/x^3 > 0 \) confirms a minimum. (3) Structure: at the optimum the two cost terms are equal (10 and 10) — the classic signature of a fixed-cost-versus-carrying-cost trade.

Answer: batch of 40; cost 20 per part; setup and carrying costs balance exactly at the optimum. Sanity check: at \( x = 30 \): \( 13.3 + 7.5 = 20.8 \); at \( x = 50 \): \( 8 + 12.5 = 20.5 \) — both worse, bracketing the minimum as they must.

quiz.q: A fabrication shop must build a closed square-base tank (base, four walls, and a lid) holding \( V = 8\ \mathrm{m^3} \). With base side \( x \) and height \( h \), the plate area is \( A = 2x^2 + 4xh \) and the constraint is \( x^2 h = 8 \). What is the minimum plate area?
quiz.solution: The constraint gives \( h = 8/x^2 \), so \( A(x) = 2x^2 + 32/x \); setting \( A'(x) = 4x - 32/x^2 = 0 \) yields \( x^3 = 8 \), hence \( x = h = 2\ \mathrm{m} \) and \( A = 8 + 16 = 24\ \mathrm{m^2} \). Since \( A''(x) = 4 + 64/x^3 \gt 0 \), this critical point is a minimum — note the closed tank optimizes to a cube, unlike the open-top case. The distractor \( 20\ \mathrm{m^2} \) is the classic slip of reusing the open-top formula \( x^2 + 4xh \) and forgetting the lid, while \( 40\ \mathrm{m^2} \) follows from mis-writing the constraint as \( xh = 8 \), which drops a dimension and gives \( h = 4\ \mathrm{m} \).

quiz.q: A cooling fan's operating cost is \( C(x) = x^2 - 8x + 20 \) (in kW-equivalent), where the speed setting \( x \) is restricted by the manufacturer to \( 0 \le x \le 3 \). What is the minimum cost achievable within the allowed range?
quiz.solution: Solving \( C'(x) = 2x - 8 = 0 \) gives \( x = 4 \), but this critical point lies outside the allowed interval, so the recipe's final step — check the ends — decides: \( C \) is decreasing on \( [0,3] \) since \( C'(x) \lt 0 \) there, and the minimum sits at the boundary, \( C(3) = 9 - 24 + 20 = 5 \). The distractor \( 4 \) is the classic error of evaluating at the unconstrained critical point \( x = 4 \) while ignoring the operating limit. Choosing \( 20 \) assumes the lowest speed is cheapest, and \( 8 \) comes from mis-solving \( 2x - 8 = 0 \) as \( x = 2 \).

quiz.q: For \( f(x) = x^3 - 12x \), the critical points are \( x = \pm 2 \). Which hosts the local maximum?
choices: Neither — the function has no local maximum
quiz.solution: \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12 = 0 \) at \( x = \pm 2 \); the second derivative \( f'' = 6x \) is negative at \( x = -2 \) (cap: local maximum, \( f(-2) = 16 \)) and positive at \( x = 2 \) (cup: local minimum, \( f(2) = -16 \)). Choosing \( x = 2 \) applies the test's sign backwards; \( x = 0 \) is where \( f'' = 0 \) — an inflection, not a critical point, since \( f'(0) = -12 \ne 0 \).

quiz.q: At a point \( x = c \), a smooth function satisfies \( f'(c) = 0 \) and \( f''(c) = 0 \). What can be concluded about \( c \)?
choices: \( c \) must be an inflection point
\( c \) must be a local minimum
Nothing yet — the second-derivative test is inconclusive, and \( c \) must be classified by the sign change of \( f' \) around it
quiz.solution: When \( f''(c) = 0 \) the second-derivative test gives no verdict: \( f(x) = x^4 \) has \( f'(0) = f''(0) = 0 \) with a genuine minimum at \( 0 \), while \( f(x) = x^3 \) satisfies the same conditions with no extremum at all, so both outcomes are possible. The reliable fallback is to examine whether \( f' \) changes sign across \( c \). The first distractor is the classic error of equating \( f'' = 0 \) with an inflection point — concavity must actually flip there, which \( x^4 \) shows it need not.

quiz.q: On a trend chart, \( f''(x) \) changes sign at \( x = c \) while \( f'(c) \neq 0 \). What is at \( c \)?
choices: An inflection point — the trend changes how it bends
quiz.solution: A sign change of the second derivative is precisely an inflection: concavity flips — a rise that was accelerating begins decelerating, or the reverse. It is not an extremum, because the first derivative is nonzero and the trend is still climbing or falling through the point; and nothing about curvature change implies a break in the function. On real trends, inflections are early news: the character of change changing is often the first visible symptom of a new regime.

6.recap:
• Curves turn where the derivative vanishes; the second derivative says whether the turn is a maximum or a minimum.
  • Optimization recipe: express the objective in one variable, differentiate, solve for stationary points — then check the endpoints.
  • Checking endpoints is not a formality. Constrained optima frequently sit at a limit rather than at a turning point, and skipping the check is the classic way to report a wrong optimum confidently.
  • The hard part is translation, not calculus: turning a stated goal into an honest objective function with its real constraints.

intro.what: A stationary point is where a quantity stops rising or falling, and that is where optima live. This lesson uses the first derivative to find candidates and the second derivative to classify them, then applies both to a design question: choosing dimensions that minimise material for a required duty.
keypoints: Optima occur where the first derivative is zero, or at the ends of the allowed range — endpoints are candidates too and are often forgotten.
The second derivative measures how the slope itself is changing, which is what distinguishes a minimum from a maximum.
Positive second derivative at a stationary point means a minimum; negative means a maximum.
An inflection is where curvature changes sign; a stationary point can be neither a maximum nor a minimum.
Real optimisation starts by writing the objective in ONE variable, using the constraint to eliminate the others.
The constraint is what makes the problem finite — without it, most engineering objectives have no interior optimum.
Check the answer is a minimum rather than assuming it; the algebra is happy to hand you a maximum.

sheets.title: Finding an optimum, and proving it is one
sheets.body:
Where a quantity is largest or smallest it is momentarily neither rising nor falling, so solving \( f'(x) = 0 \) finds stationary points. That is a search for candidates, not answers, and two habits keep it honest.

First, remember the endpoints. Physical variables are always confined — a radius cannot be negative, a pressure cannot exceed a rating — and the extreme value may sit at an end of that range where the derivative is nowhere near zero.

Second, classify what you find. The second derivative \( f''(x) \), read ‘f double prime of x’, measures how fast the slope is changing, which is curvature. At a stationary point positive means curving upwards and so a local minimum; negative means a local maximum. If it is zero the test is silent — the point may be an inflection, where curvature changes sign with no optimum at all.

Real problems arrive with several dimensions free and one requirement fixed, and the method is to use the requirement to eliminate variables. The quantity to be optimised is the objective function; the fixed requirement is the constraint. Without a constraint most engineering objectives have no interior optimum at all — the cheapest vessel is one of zero size — so the constraint is what makes the question meaningful.

The working method. Write the objective in all its variables. Write the constraint as an equation. Solve the constraint for one variable and substitute, so the objective depends on one thing. Differentiate, set to zero, solve. Classify with the second derivative and check the endpoints. Back-substitute for the other dimensions. Most of the difficulty is in the substitution step; most of the errors are in skipping the classification, which is how a maximum gets presented as a minimum.

examples.title: Least material for a required capacity, and how sharp it is
examples.body:
Problem 1. An open-top cylindrical vessel must hold \( 2\ \mathrm{m^3} \). Find the radius and height using least material, and the resulting surface area.

Approach. Objective: the area \( S \) of a base plus a wall, with no lid. Constraint: fixed volume. Eliminate the height so \( S \) depends only on \( r \). The trap is including a second circle — write the area from the actual geometry rather than recalling a closed-cylinder formula.

Solution. \( S = \pi r^2 + 2\pi rH \) with \( \pi r^2H = 2 \), so \( H = 2/(\pi r^2) \) and \( S = \pi r^2 + 4/r \). Then \( S'(r) = 2\pi r - 4/r^2 = 0 \) gives \( r^3 = 2/\pi \), \( r = 0.860\ \mathrm{m} \); \( S''(r) = 2\pi + 8/r^3 = 18.85 > 0 \), a minimum; and \( H = 0.860\ \mathrm{m} \).

Answer. \( r = H = 0.860\ \mathrm{m} \), \( S = 6.97\ \mathrm{m^2} \). Height equals radius exactly, whatever volume is required.

Problem 2. Evaluate the area at \( r = 0.70 \) and \( r = 1.00\ \mathrm{m} \) and comment on how sharp the optimum is.

Approach. The second-derivative test proves a minimum but says nothing about how much it matters. Evaluating nearby answers the practical question: how much material is lost by building a little off optimum. That decides whether the optimisation survives contact with a stock size.

Solution. \( S = \pi r^2 + 4/r \) gives \( 1.539 + 5.714 = 7.254 \) at 0.70, and \( 3.142 + 4.000 = 7.142 \) at 1.00, against 6.975 at the optimum.

Answer. Both neighbours cost more, confirming the minimum, but only by 4.0% and 2.4%. The optimum is shallow, so rounding to a stock radius costs very little.

7.lecture:
§1 · Accumulation is the other half of calculus

The derivative asks: how fast? The integral asks the inverse question: how much, in total? A flow meter reads m³/h instant by instant; the invoice wants m³. Adding up a changing rate over time is integration — the total volume \( V \) that passes in the time from \( 0 \) to \( T \), accumulated from the instantaneous volumetric flow rate \( Q(t) \):

\[ V = \int_{0}^{T} Q(t)\,dt \tag{1} \]

Geometrically this is the area under the \( Q(t) \) curve — approximated by stacking thin rectangles \( Q \cdot \Delta t \) and letting \( \Delta t \to 0 \). Every totalizer in the plant is performing equation (1) in silicon, all day long.

§2 · The Fundamental Theorem — rates and totals are inverses

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says accumulation and differentiation undo each other: if \( F(t) = \int_a^t f(x)\,dx \), then \( F' = f \). Consequently

\[ \int_a^b f(t)\,dt = F(b) - F(a) \quad\text{where } F' = f \tag{2} \]

Find any antiderivative, evaluate at the ends, subtract. The theorem is why energy (kWh) is the antiderivative of power (kW), why distance is the antiderivative of speed, and why a totalizer can be checked against two readings of a cumulative register.

§3 · Reading areas like an engineer

Area under a pump's power trend = energy consumed. Area under a flow curve = volume transferred. Area between inflow and outflow curves = inventory change. When the curve is data rather than formula, the integral is done numerically — trapezoids on historian samples — which is Lesson 9's business. The concept is identical: total = area.

§4 · Setting up an integral — the working method

Every accumulation problem is set up the same way, and the setup is where the marks are won or lost. Identify the rate — the quantity per time (or per length, per angle) being accumulated — and write its units down. Fix the interval: the start and end of the accumulation, in the rate's own time variable. Integrate, and check the units of the result: a rate in m³/h integrated over hours must land in m³, and if it doesn't, the setup — not the arithmetic — is wrong. Then exploit the Fundamental Theorem in both directions. Given a formula, find an antiderivative and evaluate at the ends. Given a cumulative register — a totalizer, an energy meter, an odometer — the theorem says the accumulation over any window is simply the difference of two readings: engineering's most underrated free lunch.

Sketch first, always. A rough graph of the rate shows whether the answer should be near the peak-times-width rectangle or well under it, whether any region runs negative, and where the accumulation concentrates. The sketch is the estimate, the integral is the precision, and disagreement between them is the error alarm that catches transposed limits and dropped signs before they reach a report.

One caution completes the method: an integral answers exactly the question its limits ask, no more. A total over a shift says nothing about which hour did the accumulating, and a net accumulation of zero can hide furious movement in both directions. Keep the question and the interval welded together when you present the number, and totals stop being ambushed by follow-up questions.

Closing. Integrals accumulate rates into totals; the Fundamental Theorem makes them computable from antiderivatives; and the plant's totalizers, energy meters, and inventory balances are integrals with tag numbers.

7.kuwait: Vignette — the invoice audit. You arrive at a monthly utilities meeting where a neighboring consumer disputes the demineralized-water charge: "our line only draws 30 m³/h." The historian's flow trend says the line ramps hard every startup. You export the week's \( Q(t) \), integrate numerically, and the area under the curve says 5,410 m³ against their flat-rate claim of 5,040. The 7% difference is startup ramps — invisible to anyone quoting instantaneous flow, undeniable to anyone who owns equation (1). The invoice stands, with a trend chart attached.

quiz.q:
Volume from a ramping flow

Problem. During a transfer, flow ramps as \( Q(t) = 20 + 4t \) m³/h (\( t \) in hours) for six hours. Find: the total volume moved.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( V = \int_0^6 (20+4t)\,dt \). (2) Antiderivative: \( 20t + 2t^2 \). (3) Evaluate: \( (120 + 72) - 0 = 192\ \mathrm{m^3} \).

Answer: 192 m³. Sanity check: average flow is \( (20+44)/2 = 32\ \mathrm{m^3/h} \) over 6 h → 192 m³. The trapezoid agrees with the antiderivative, as it must for a linear ramp.

quiz.q:
Energy from a power trend

Problem. A compressor's electrical demand across a shift is modeled \( P(t) = 250 - 10t + t^2 \) kW over \( 0 \le t \le 8 \) h. Find: the energy consumed and the average power.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( E = \int_0^8 (250 - 10t + t^2)\,dt = \left[250t - 5t^2 + t^3/3\right]_0^8 \). (2) \( = 2000 - 320 + 170.7 = 1850.7\ \mathrm{kWh} \). (3) Average power \( = E/8 = 231.3\ \mathrm{kW} \).

Answer: ≈1851 kWh; average ≈231 kW. Sanity check: the parabola dips mid-shift (minimum \( P(5) = 225 \) kW) and ends at \( P(8)=234 \); an average of 231 kW sits sensibly between the minimum and the endpoints.

quiz.q:
Auditing a week from two register readings

Problem. A water totalizer — a cumulative register, i.e. an antiderivative of flow — read 10,450 m³ on Monday 08:00 and 12,730 m³ on Friday 08:00 (96 hours later). Find: the volume consumed and the true average flow for the period, and name the theorem doing the work.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) By the Fundamental Theorem, consumption over the window is the register difference: \( 12{,}730 - 10{,}450 = 2{,}280\ \mathrm{m^3} \) — no flow curve needed. (2) True average flow: \( 2{,}280/96 = 23.75\ \mathrm{m^3/h} \). (3) The register is \( F(t) \) with \( F' = Q \); two readings evaluate \( \int Q\,dt \) exactly, whatever the flow did in between.

Answer: 2,280 m³; 23.75 m³/h average. Sanity check: a line that idles nights could still spike far above 23.75 by day — the average from registers is exact as an average, and silent about peaks; that distinction is the next lesson's business.

quiz.q: During a controlled draw-down, a tank's outflow falls linearly as \( Q(t) = 50 - 4t \ \mathrm{m^3/h} \) for \( 0 \le t \le 6 \) h. What total volume leaves the tank during the six hours?
quiz.solution: Volume is the accumulated rate: \( \int_0^6 (50-4t)\,dt = \left[50t - 2t^2\right]_0^6 = 300 - 72 = 228\ \mathrm{m^3} \). The distractor 156 m³ comes from the classic antiderivative slip of writing \( 50t - 4t^2 \), forgetting to divide by the new power when reversing the power rule. The distractor 300 m³ multiplies the initial rate by the duration as if the flow never declined, ignoring that the integrand changes over the interval.

quiz.q: A pump motor's electrical demand over a 4-hour run is modeled by \( P(t) = 120 + 30t - 3t^2 \) kW. What is the average power drawn over the run?
quiz.solution: Energy is the area under the power curve: \( E = \int_0^4 (120 + 30t - 3t^2)\,dt = \left[120t + 15t^2 - t^3\right]_0^4 = 656\ \mathrm{kWh} \), and the average power is that total divided by the interval, \( 656/4 = 164\ \mathrm{kW} \). Choosing 656 confuses the integral (kWh) with its average (kW) — a unit slip that forgets the division by the 4 h duration. The distractor 156 kW is the endpoint average \( (P(0)+P(4))/2 = (120+192)/2 \), which only equals the true average when the curve is linear; this parabola bulges above its chord.

quiz.q: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_1^3 (2t + 1)\,dt \).
quiz.solution: The antiderivative is \( t^2 + t \); evaluating, \( (9 + 3) - (1 + 1) = 10 \). Answering 14 forgets to subtract the lower-end value — the most common definite-integral slip; 22 is the integrand's value at \( t=3 \) times the width, treating a changing rate as constant at its end value. The average-rate check: the integrand runs from 3 to 7, averaging 5 over width 2 — exactly 10.

quiz.q: Historian tags record a tank's inflow \( Q_{\text{in}}(t) \) and outflow \( Q_{\text{out}}(t) \), both in \( \mathrm{m^3/h} \). What physical quantity does \( \int_0^T \big[ Q_{\text{in}}(t) - Q_{\text{out}}(t) \big]\,dt \) equal?
choices: The change in stored volume between \( t=0 \) and \( t=T \), in \( \mathrm{m^3} \)
The tank's absolute liquid volume at \( t=T \), in \( \mathrm{m^3} \)
The instantaneous net inflow at \( t=T \), in \( \mathrm{m^3/h} \)
The average net inflow rate over the interval, in \( \mathrm{m^3/h} \)
quiz.solution: The integrand \( Q_{\text{in}} - Q_{\text{out}} \) is the net rate of accumulation, so by the Fundamental Theorem its definite integral over \( [0,T] \) is the net volume added — the inventory change \( V(T) - V(0) \), in \( \mathrm{m^3} \). It is not the absolute volume at \( t=T \): that classic error forgets the initial inventory \( V(0) \), which the definite integral cannot see. The remaining options confuse the integral with its integrand (a rate at one instant) or with the average rate, which would require dividing the integral by \( T \).

quiz.q: During a filter backflush, a line's flow \( Q(t) \) runs negative for part of an interval. What does \( \int Q\,dt \) over that interval report?
choices: The net volume delivered, with backflow counted negative
The gross volume that moved in either direction
Zero — integrals of negative regions are discarded
quiz.solution: The definite integral is signed area: forward flow accumulates positive, reverse flow negative, and the result is net delivery — which is exactly what an inventory balance needs. Gross movement would require integrating \( |Q| \), a different (and occasionally also useful) quantity. Discarding negative regions is not a convention mathematics offers, and an average is the integral divided by the width, not the integral itself.

7.recap:
• The derivative asks how fast; the integral asks how much in total. They are the two halves of the subject.
  • \( V = \int_0^T Q(t)\,dt \) — every totalizer in the plant is performing this calculation continuously.
  • Fundamental Theorem: accumulation and differentiation undo each other, so \( \int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a) \). Find any antiderivative and evaluate at the two ends.
  • Area under a curve is a physical total. Read the units of the area to know which total it is: rate × time is quantity, force × distance is work.

intro.what: Differentiation asks how fast something changes; integration asks how much has accumulated. If you know a rate and want a total — a flow and want a volume, a power and want an energy, a corrosion rate and want a wall loss — the operation you need is a definite integral. This lesson builds it as a limit of sums and reads it as an area.
keypoints: Integrating a rate over an interval gives the total accumulated over that interval, in the rate's units multiplied by the interval's.
A definite integral is defined as the limit of a sum of narrow strips, which is why it equals the area under the curve.
The area interpretation is literal: strip width times strip height, summed.
Areas below the axis count as negative, so an integral can represent a net rather than a gross total.
The Fundamental Theorem links the two halves of calculus: integrate a rate by finding a function whose derivative is that rate.
The average value of a quantity over an interval is its integral divided by the interval length.
A numerical sum with finitely many strips approaches the exact integral as the strips narrow — which is how instruments actually totalise.

sheets.title: Accumulating a rate: sums, integrals and averages
sheets.body:
If a flow varies through a shift and you need the volume passed, chop the shift into short intervals, treat the rate as constant across each, multiply and add. That is a Riemann sum \( \sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x \), where \( \Delta x \) is one interval's width. Each term is a rectangle: a height from the curve, a width from the interval. It is wrong by however much the rate moved inside each interval.

Narrow the intervals and that error shrinks. The definite integral \( \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \), read ‘the integral from a to b of f of x d x’, is what the sum approaches as the strips become arbitrarily narrow. The elongated S is a sum sign and \( dx \) is the vanishing width, so the notation pictures the construction.

Two consequences follow at once. The integral is the area under the curve, because that is literally what was summed — and area below the axis counts negative, so an integral of a signed quantity gives a net, not a gross, total. And the units follow the multiplication: cubic metres per second integrated over seconds gives cubic metres.

Summing strips converges but is laborious. The exact route is the Fundamental Theorem, \( \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) \), where the antiderivative \( F \) is any function whose derivative is the integrand. Integration is differentiation run backwards, which is why the earlier rules are not left behind.

The integral also delivers the average value, \( \bar{f} = \dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx \) — the constant value that would accumulate the same total in the same time. That is not the mean of a handful of readings: readings taken at uneven intervals, or while the quantity moved quickly, give a different and generally wrong answer, because the integral weights every instant by how long it actually lasted.

examples.title: Volume from a ramping flow, and a sum converging to it
examples.body:
Problem 1. During start-up a flow rises as \( Q(t) = 0.05 + 0.01t \), \( Q \) in \( \mathrm{m^3/s} \), \( t \) in seconds. Find the volume passed in 60 s and the average flow.

Approach. Volume is the accumulation of flow, so integrate the rate over the interval; the antiderivative is immediate. The error to avoid is multiplying the final flow by elapsed time, which treats a ramp as though it ran at maximum throughout and overstates the volume by more than half.

Solution. \( F(t) = 0.05t + 0.005t^2 \), whose derivative is the integrand, so \( F(60) - F(0) = 3.0 + 18.0 \). The average is that total divided by 60.

Answer. 21.0 m³ at an average of 0.35 m³/s. The wrong method gives 39 m³. The average equals the flow at the midpoint, 30 s, which is a property of a linear ramp.

Problem 2. Approximate the same volume with left-endpoint sums of 6, 60 and 600 strips.

Approach. A left-endpoint sum takes each strip's height at the start of its interval, which for a rising rate is the lowest value in the strip — so every rectangle sits below the curve and the sum must under-estimate. Predicting the direction before computing is the point. This is how a flow totaliser accumulates from periodic samples.

Solution. With \( \Delta t = 10, 1 \) and \( 0.1\ \mathrm{s} \) the sums are 18.0, 20.7 and 20.97 m³.

Answer. Always low, as predicted, closing on 21.0. Each tenfold increase in strip count cuts the error tenfold — 3.0, 0.3, 0.03 — so a totaliser sampling once a second here under-reads by about 1.4%.

8.lecture:
§1 · Substitution — the chain rule reversed

Most integrals you meet are chain-rule results wearing a disguise. Substitution unmasks them: set \( u = \) the inner function, trade \( dx \) for \( du \), integrate, return.

\[ \int x\,(x^2+1)^3 dx \;\xrightarrow{\,u = x^2+1,\ du = 2x\,dx\,}\; \tfrac12\int u^3 du = \frac{(x^2+1)^4}{8} + C \tag{1} \]

The skill is seeing the derivative of the inside sitting beside it. Flow, decay, and geometry integrals in plant work overwhelmingly fall to substitution.

§2 · Integration by parts — the product rule reversed

When the integrand is a genuine product — a polynomial times an exponential, say — parts applies:

\[ \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du \tag{2} \]

Choose \( u \) to simplify when differentiated, \( dv \) to stay tame when integrated. The workhorse case \( \int t\,e^{-t}dt \) models energy in decaying transients and first-moment calculations, and §Worked Examples runs it end to end.

§3 · Knowing when to stop

Real plant data rarely hands you a clean antiderivative. The professional sequence is: try substitution; try parts; recognize a table form; otherwise integrate numerically — trapezoids or Simpson on sampled data — and say so. A numerically honest answer beats a heroic symbolic detour every time. Software does symbolic work well; your job is to set the integral up correctly and sanity-check its output.

§4 · Choosing the technique — a decision procedure

Integration is pattern recognition with a fallback ladder, and the ladder has exactly four rungs. Rung one: is the derivative of an inner function sitting beside it? If the integrand contains \( g(x) \) inside another function and \( g'(x) \) — up to a constant — as a factor, substitution finishes it in one line. Train the eye on the constant: in \( \int x\,e^{x^2}dx \), the \( x \) outside is \( \tfrac12 \) of the needed \( 2x \), and the half simply rides along. Rung two: a genuine product of unrelated factors — polynomial times exponential, polynomial times sine — goes to parts, choosing \( u \) as the factor that simplifies when differentiated. Rung three: recognize a table form and write the answer. Rung four: integrate numerically — trapezoids on the samples you have — and say so plainly.

Two habits turn technique into reliability. Verify every antiderivative by differentiating it — ten seconds that catch dropped halves and sign slips before they propagate. And when limits are involved in a substitution, transform them with the variable so the evaluation happens in \( u \)-space and nothing needs converting back. The techniques are few; the discipline around them is what makes the answers dependable.

Know also what the ladder is for. In professional work, symbolic software integrates faster than any human — but it cannot decide whether the integral was set up correctly, whether the limits mean what the question meant, or whether the answer's magnitude is plausible. The techniques you practice here build exactly that judgment: someone who has integrated by hand recognizes a wrong machine answer on sight, the way a machinist who has cut threads manually reads a bad CNC part at a glance. Learn the moves to own the judgment, then delegate the labor freely.

Closing. Substitution reverses the chain rule, parts reverses the product rule, and numerical integration is the licensed fallback — not a defeat.

  • Exponentials (Lesson 5) — \( \int e^{kt}dt = e^{kt}/k + C \) appears constantly.

Glossary

8.kuwait: Vignette — the totalizer that lied politely. You arrive to commission a batching skid whose vendor totalizer disagrees with the tank dip by 4% every batch. The vendor's firmware integrates flow with coarse rectangles at a slow scan; the batch flow rises and falls steeply. You re-integrate a logged batch with trapezoids — thirty minutes in a spreadsheet — and land within 0.5% of the dip. The finding isn't "the meter is bad"; it's "the integration method under-resolves the ramps." The vendor pushes a firmware setting, scan tightens, and the totalizer and the tank finally tell one story. Technique matters even when silicon does the arithmetic.

quiz.q:
Substitution with limits

Problem. Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 x\,(x^2+1)^3\,dx \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( u = x^2+1 \), \( du = 2x\,dx \); limits map \( x{=}0 \to u{=}1 \), \( x{=}2 \to u{=}5 \). (2) Integral becomes \( \tfrac12 \int_1^5 u^3 du = \tfrac12 \cdot \frac{u^4}{4}\Big|_1^5 \). (3) \( = \frac{625 - 1}{8} = 78 \).

Answer: 78. Sanity check: the integrand at \( x=2 \) is \( 2 \times 125 = 250 \), at 0 it's 0; a rough average of ~40 over width 2 gives ~80 — same neighborhood as 78.

quiz.q:
Parts on a decaying transient

Problem. A quantity accumulates as \( \int_0^2 t\,e^{-t}\,dt \) (dimensionless model of energy delivered by a decaying pulse). Find: its value.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Parts with \( u = t,\ dv = e^{-t}dt \Rightarrow du = dt,\ v = -e^{-t} \). (2) \( \int t e^{-t} dt = -t e^{-t} + \int e^{-t} dt = -t e^{-t} - e^{-t} \). (3) Evaluate 0→2: \( \left[-(t+1)e^{-t}\right]_0^2 = -(3)(0.1353) + 1 = 1 - 0.406 = 0.594 \).

Answer: ≈0.594. Sanity check: the full integral to infinity equals 1 exactly; by \( t=2 \) (two time constants) most of the pulse has landed — 59% here, with the tail's remainder consistent with \( (t+1)e^{-t} \) at \( t=2 \) being 0.406.

quiz.q:
Integrating data that has no formula

Problem. A flow is sampled every 15 minutes: 40, 52, 60, 54, 42 m³/h. Find: the volume transferred over the hour by the trapezoid rule.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Step \( h = 0.25 \) h. Trapezoid rule: \( V = h\left[\tfrac{f_0 + f_4}{2} + f_1 + f_2 + f_3\right] \). (2) \( V = 0.25\left[\tfrac{40+42}{2} + 52 + 60 + 54\right] = 0.25\,(41 + 166) = 51.75\ \mathrm{m^3} \).

Answer: ≈51.8 m³. Sanity check: the flow averaged roughly 50 m³/h over one hour, so ~50 m³ is the expected neighborhood; the trapezoid answer sits just above it because the curve spends more time near its 60 m³/h crest than at its ends. This is rung four of the technique ladder — used openly, it is not an approximation of last resort but the standard tool for sampled data.

quiz.q: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 \frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx \).
quiz.solution: Set \( u = x^2+1 \), so \( du = 2x\,dx \) and the limits map to \( u=1 \) and \( u=5 \), giving \( \tfrac12\int_1^5 \frac{du}{u} = \tfrac12\ln 5 \). The answer \( \ln 5 \) is the most common substitution slip: dropping the factor \( \tfrac12 \) that \( du = 2x\,dx \) forces. \( \arctan 2 \) comes from pattern-matching the table form \( \int dx/(x^2+1) \) while ignoring the \( x \) in the numerator, and \( \tfrac12\ln 3 \) results from converting the upper limit as \( 2+1 \) instead of \( 2^2+1 \).

quiz.q: Using integration by parts, evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^1 x\,e^{x}\,dx \).
quiz.solution: Take \( u = x \), \( dv = e^x dx \), so \( \int x e^x dx = x e^x - \int e^x dx = (x-1)e^x \); evaluating from 0 to 1 gives \( 0 - (-1) = 1 \). The value \( e/2 \) is the classic error of integrating the two factors independently as \( (x^2/2)e^x \) — integration has no product rule, which is exactly why parts exists. \( 2e-1 \) follows from a sign slip in the parts formula (writing \( uv + \int v\,du \)), and \( e-1 \) is \( \int_0^1 e^x dx \) alone, i.e., forgetting the boundary term \( uv \).

quiz.q: What is \( \displaystyle\int e^{3t}\,dt \)?
quiz.solution: Differentiating \( \tfrac13 e^{3t} \) returns \( e^{3t} \) — the inner derivative 3 must be divided away, not multiplied in. Choosing \( 3e^{3t} \) applies the chain rule in the forward direction, the classic inversion error; the ten-second audit — differentiate your answer — catches it instantly. The \( t\,e^{3t} \) option imports a factor that only appears when integrating products by parts, not plain exponentials.

quiz.q: Each integrand below is a polynomial factor times an exponential or composite factor. For which integral does substitution alone fail, making integration by parts the required technique?
quiz.solution: Substitution works only when the derivative of the inner function sits beside it: in \( \int x e^{x^2} dx \), \( \int x^2 e^{x^3} dx \), and \( \int 2x/(x^2+1)\,dx \) the polynomial factor is, up to a constant, the derivative of the inner function, so a \( u \)-substitution finishes each in one line. In \( \int x e^{3x} dx \) the inner function \( 3x \) has constant derivative, so the leftover \( x \) cannot be absorbed into \( du \); the integrand is a genuine product and parts applies. The classic error runs the other way: seeing \( x \) times an exponential in \( \int x e^{x^2} dx \) and launching into parts, which only produces a harder integral.

quiz.q: Which is \( \displaystyle\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx \)?
quiz.solution: The derivative of the inner function \( x^2 \) is \( 2x \), sitting right there as a factor — substitution territory: \( u = x^2 \) gives \( \int\cos u\,du = \sin u + C = \sin(x^2) + C \). Check by differentiating: \( \tfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = 2x\cos(x^2) \) ✓. The \( \cos(x^3/3) \) option "integrates the inside," a move calculus never licenses; the sign-flipped option confuses the sine and cosine derivative pair.

8.recap:
• Substitution is the chain rule run backwards — look for a function and its own derivative sitting in the same integrand.
  • Integration by parts is the product rule run backwards: \( \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du \). Choose \( u \) to be the factor that simplifies when differentiated.
  • Know when to stop. Many perfectly ordinary integrals have no closed form, and a numerical answer is a legitimate engineering answer, not a defeat.

intro.what: Most integrals met in engineering are not in any table. Two techniques cover the great majority: substitution, which reverses the chain rule, and integration by parts, which reverses the product rule. Each is a differentiation rule read backwards, which is also how you decide which one a given integral needs.
keypoints: Substitution reverses the chain rule: look for an inner function whose derivative also appears as a factor.
When substituting in a definite integral, change the limits too, or convert back before evaluating — never mix the two.
Integration by parts reverses the product rule and is the tool for a product of unlike things, such as a power multiplied by an exponential.
The choice of which factor to differentiate decides whether the new integral is easier or worse; pick the one that simplifies when differentiated.
By parts may need repeating, and each pass should visibly reduce the difficulty.
Every indefinite integral carries an arbitrary constant, which cancels in a definite integral and matters in a differential equation.
Check any integration by differentiating the answer — it is fast and it is conclusive.

sheets.title: Substitution and by parts: two rules read backwards
sheets.body:
Differentiating a function of a function multiplies by the inner derivative, so integration must divide it out again. Substitution is the bookkeeping that does so safely.

The pattern to recognise is an integrand containing an inner expression together with that expression's own derivative as a factor. Name the inner expression \( u = g(x) \), form the differential \( du = g'(x)\,dx \), and the integral rewrites in \( u \) alone. If the derivative is absent, up to a constant multiple, substitution is the wrong tool and forcing it produces nonsense.

For a definite integral there are two honest routes and one common error. Either convert the limits into the new variable, or keep the old limits and convert back before substituting them. The error is to change the variable and keep the original limits, which evaluates the right function at the wrong points.

The product rule reversed gives integration by parts, \( \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du \). It does not evaluate an integral outright; it trades one for another, and is worth using only when the trade is favourable. That makes the choice of \( u \) the whole skill: the factor you name \( u \) gets differentiated, so choose the one that simplifies. A power is the usual choice because differentiating lowers it; an exponential is the usual \( dv \) because integrating changes nothing. Choosing the other way round is not wrong so much as useless — if one application leaves you worse off, swap the roles rather than pressing on.

Every indefinite integral carries a constant of integration \( C \), because differentiation destroys constants. It cancels between limits and matters in a differential equation, which is two lessons ahead. Whatever technique is used, the check takes seconds: differentiate the answer and confirm the integrand returns.

examples.title: A substitution with changed limits, and a decaying transient
examples.body:
Problem 1. Evaluate \( \int_0^2 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx \).

Approach. The exponent \( x^2 \) is an inner function and its derivative \( 2x \) sits there as a factor — the signature of a substitution. Change the limits with the variable: as \( x \) runs 0 to 2, \( u \) runs 0 to 4. Keeping the original limits would evaluate between 0 and 2 instead, giving 6.39: a plausible number with nothing visibly wrong.

Solution. \( u = x^2 \), \( du = 2x\,dx \), so the integral is \( \int_0^4 e^{u}\,du = e^{u}\big|_0^4 = e^4 - 1 \).

Answer. 53.598. Differentiating \( e^{x^2} \) returns \( 2x\,e^{x^2} \), confirming it.

Problem 2. Evaluate \( \int_0^{10} t\,e^{-t/5}\,dt \).

Approach. A power times an exponential: substitution cannot help, since the exponent's derivative is a constant and not the other factor. Use by parts with \( u = t \), so differentiating reduces it to 1. Taking \( u = e^{-t/5} \) instead leaves \( t^2/2 \) — a higher power than you started with, the signal to swap roles.

Solution. With \( dv = e^{-t/5}\,dt \), \( v = -5e^{-t/5} \), giving \( \left[-5t\,e^{-t/5}\right]_0^{10} + 5\int_0^{10} e^{-t/5}\,dt = -6.767 + 21.617 \).

Answer. 14.850, confirmed by a numerical midpoint sum at 14.8499. The first term is negative and the second positive, which is normal here.

9.lecture:
§1 · Average value — what the meter should have read

The average of a continuously varying quantity is its integral spread evenly across the interval:

\[ \bar f = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(t)\,dt \tag{1} \]

Average demand, average flow, average temperature — every KPI that begins with the word "average" is equation (1), whether computed honestly or not. When someone averages three spot readings taken at convenient times, you now know precisely what they did wrong.

§2 · RMS — the average that heats

Electrical heating goes as the square of current, so the meaningful "average" for AC is the root of the mean of the square:

\[ f_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f^2(t)\,dt}, \qquad \text{for } f = A\sin\omega t:\ f_{rms} = \frac{A}{\sqrt 2} \tag{2} \]

The sine result follows because \( \sin^2 \) averages to exactly ½ over a cycle. This is why 230 V mains has a 325 V peak, and why vibration severity standards quote RMS velocity: RMS tracks energy, and energy does the damage.

§3 · Work by integration

When force varies along the path, work is accumulated force-times-distance: \( W = \int F\,dx \). Pumping a tank empty is the signature case: each layer of liquid at depth \( y \) has weight \( \rho g A\,dy \) — density \( \rho \) times gravitational acceleration \( g \) times the tank's cross-sectional area \( A \) times the layer's own thickness \( dy \) — and must rise a different height. Summing layers is an integral, executed in §Worked Examples for a real tank. The same layer-summing pattern computes hydrostatic forces on gates and centroids of plates — one method, many billables.

§4 · Choosing the right average — a field guide

Three different averages answer three different questions, and choosing the wrong one is a quiet, expensive error. The plain mean — equation (1) — answers "how much per unit time on the invoice": billing, throughput, duty totals. The RMS — equation (2) — answers "what steady level would heat, stress, or wear the same": electrical heating, vibration severity, fatigue-relevant loading, because damage physics runs on squares. The peak answers "will it survive the worst instant": trips, relief sizing, insulation. A signal has all three numbers at once, and the crest factor — peak over RMS — is the single figure that says how far apart they live: near 1.4 for a clean sine, climbing whenever impacts and spikes enter, which is why analysts watch it as an early bearing-damage flag.

On sampled data the integrals become sums without changing meaning: mean the samples for equation (1), mean the squares and take the root for equation (2), weighting by interval when the sampling is uneven. For work-by-layers problems, the recipe is mechanical: draw the layer, write its weight, write its travel distance as a function of position, integrate over the geometry — then check against the centroid shortcut, which agrees every time the geometry is uniform and catches the setup when it isn't.

The same layer-summing pattern prices hydrostatic force on a gate, the metal in a tapered column, and the moment of a distributed load — one method, many invoices. What changes between problems is only what each layer carries: weight, pressure, or load per metre. Master the pattern once, in the tank problem, and every later course that says "integrate over the geometry" is asking for a rerun.

Closing. Integrals define honest averages (1), energy-true averages (2), and path-dependent work — three tools that turn "roughly" into "defensibly."

9.kuwait: Vignette — the average that wasn't. You arrive at a demand-charge dispute: the utility bills on average kW over each 15-minute window, and the plant's spreadsheet — three manual readings a shift — says the plant never crosses the contract limit. The historian's one-minute data, run through equation (1) per window, says otherwise: startup windows average 8% over. The spreadsheet sampled politely between the peaks. Billing is an integral; sampling is an opinion. The plant reschedules two big starts and the penalty disappears next cycle.

quiz.q:
RMS of a sine, derived

Problem. Show \( f_{rms} = A/\sqrt2 \) for \( f = A\sin\omega t \) over one period.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( f^2 = A^2\sin^2\omega t = \frac{A^2}{2}(1 - \cos 2\omega t) \). (2) The cosine term integrates to zero over a full period, so \( \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f^2 dt = \frac{A^2}{2} \). (3) Square root: \( f_{rms} = A/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707A \).

Answer: \( A/\sqrt2 \). Sanity check: 230 V RMS × √2 = 325 V peak — the familiar mains numbers reproduce.

quiz.q:
Emptying a tank over the rim

Problem. A vertical cylindrical water tank, radius 1.5 m, holds 4.0 m of water. Find: the minimum work to pump the entire contents over the rim (at the 4.0 m level).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Layer at height \( y \) (from the bottom), thickness \( dy \): volume \( A\,dy \) with \( A = \pi(1.5)^2 = 7.07\ \mathrm{m^2} \); lift height \( (4-y) \). (2) \( W = \rho g A \int_0^4 (4-y)\,dy = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 7.07 \times \left[4y - \tfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^4 \). (3) Bracket: \( 16 - 8 = 8 \). So \( W = 69{,}300 \times 8 = 555\ \mathrm{kJ} \).

Answer: ≈555 kJ (≈0.154 kWh). Sanity check: total mass 28.3 t lifted an average of 2 m: \( 28{,}300 \times 9.81 \times 2 = 555\ \mathrm{kJ} \) — the centroid shortcut confirms the integral exactly.

quiz.q:
Mean versus RMS on a duty cycle

Problem. A motor draws 40 A for 2 s, then 10 A for 8 s, repeating every 10 s. Find: the mean current and the RMS current, and state which one sizes the motor thermally.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Mean: \( (40 \times 2 + 10 \times 8)/10 = 160/10 = 16\ \mathrm{A} \). (2) RMS: mean of squares \( = (40^2 \times 2 + 10^2 \times 8)/10 = (3200 + 800)/10 = 400 \), so \( I_{rms} = 20\ \mathrm{A} \). (3) Heating goes as \( I^2R \), so the 20 A figure — not 16 A — is the thermally equivalent steady current.

Answer: mean 16 A, RMS 20 A; thermal sizing uses RMS. Sanity check: RMS ≥ mean always, with equality only for constant signals; a motor sized on the 16 A average would run 56% hot on an \( I^2 \) basis \( (400/256 = 1.56) \) — the exact mistake the RMS concept exists to prevent.

quiz.q: A reactor jacket temperature follows \( T(t) = 20 + 4t - t^2 \) (in Celsius, with \( t \) in hours) over a 3-hour batch, \( 0 \le t \le 3 \). What is the true mean temperature of the batch?
quiz.solution: The mean value is \( \bar T = \frac{1}{3}\int_0^3 (20 + 4t - t^2)\,dt = \frac{1}{3}\left[20t + 2t^2 - \tfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = \frac{69}{3} = 23.0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} \). Averaging only the start and end readings gives 21.5 °C — the spot-reading shortcut the lecture warns against, which misses everything between the samples. Choosing 69 °C is the integral itself, forgetting to divide by the interval width \( b-a \); 23.75 °C is a single reading at the midpoint, another form of spot sampling.

quiz.q: A vertical cylindrical tank of radius 1.0 m holds water (\( \rho = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \)) to a depth of 3.0 m. Taking \( g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), what is the minimum work required to pump the entire contents over the rim at the 3.0 m level?
quiz.solution: A layer at height \( y \) has weight \( \rho g A\,dy \) with \( A = \pi(1.0)^2 \) and must rise \( (3-y) \), so \( W = \rho g A \int_0^3 (3-y)\,dy = 1000 \times 9.81 \times \pi \times 4.5 \approx 139\ \mathrm{kJ} \). The centroid shortcut confirms it: 9.42 t of water rising 1.5 m gives the same 139 kJ. Choosing 277 kJ lifts the whole mass through the full 3.0 m instead of the centroid height — the classic error of ignoring that each layer travels a different distance; 14.1 kJ drops \( g \), leaving mass-metres rather than joules.

quiz.q: What is the mean value of \( f(t) = 6t^2 \) over \( [0, 2] \)?
quiz.solution: \( \bar f = \tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^2 6t^2 dt = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[2t^3\right]_0^2 = \tfrac{16}{2} = 8 \). Answering 16 is the integral without dividing by the width — a total, not an average; 24 is the endpoint value \( f(2) \), the spot-reading error; 4 halves the correct answer by dividing twice. Mean value is always integral over width: the two operations are inseparable.

quiz.q: Why does the RMS value, rather than the plain time-average, represent the heating effect of an AC current in a resistor?
choices: Instantaneous dissipation scales as the square of the current, and the plain mean of a symmetric sinusoid over a cycle is zero, so only the mean of the squared signal tracks the energy delivered.
The RMS of any waveform equals its peak divided by \( \sqrt{2} \), which makes it directly comparable to a DC value.
RMS equals the mean of the absolute value of the current, which is the quantity a heating element responds to.
RMS is always larger than the plain mean, so it builds a conservative safety margin into thermal ratings.
quiz.solution: Power in a resistor is \( i^2 R \), so the physically meaningful average must be taken on \( i^2 \); the square root then restores current units, giving the DC-equivalent amplitude that produces the same heating. The \( \sqrt{2} \) relation in the second choice is the classic overgeneralisation — peak divided by \( \sqrt{2} \) holds only for pure sinusoids, and the crest factor of other waveforms differs. The third choice confuses RMS with the rectified (mean-absolute) average, a distinct and generally smaller quantity.

quiz.q: Which signal has a crest factor of exactly \( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 \)?
choices: An impulsive signal with sharp spikes
quiz.solution: For a sine, peak \( = A \) and RMS \( = A/\sqrt2 \), so peak/RMS \( = \sqrt2 \). A constant and a square wave both have RMS equal to their peak — crest factor 1 — while impulsive signals push the ratio well above 2, which is precisely why a rising crest factor on a bearing's vibration flags early impact-type damage while the RMS still looks calm. Crest factor is the one number that says how "spiky" a signal is.

9.recap:
• Average value is the integral spread evenly across the interval. Every KPI beginning with the word "average" is this calculation — whether or not it was computed honestly.
  • Averaging a few spot readings taken at convenient times is not this calculation, and you can now say precisely why.
  • RMS is the average that heats. Electrical heating goes as the square of current, so the meaningful average for an alternating quantity is the root of the mean of the square — which is why vibration severity standards quote RMS velocity.
  • Work by integration when force varies along the path: \( W = \int F\,dx \). Emptying a tank is the signature case, because each layer must rise a different height.
  • Choosing the right average — mean, RMS, or time-weighted — is a field decision with different answers, not a matter of taste.

intro.what: Integration earns its keep when the thing being accumulated is not a rate in time. Areas between curves, volumes of revolution, work against a varying force and true averages are all the same operation applied to different integrands. This lesson is about choosing the integrand correctly, which is where the engineering sits.
keypoints: Every application is the same construction: slice the object, write one slice's contribution, then integrate.
Getting the slice right is the whole problem; the integration afterwards is routine.
Work is force integrated over distance, and it needs an integral exactly when the force varies.
For pumping problems the varying quantity is usually the lift, not the weight of the slice.
The average value of a quantity is its integral divided by the interval, not the mean of a few readings.
Root-mean-square is a different average again — square, average, then take the root, in that order.
For a sinusoid the RMS value is the peak divided by root two, which is why AC quantities are quoted that way.
